def: An integrin on leukocytes that binds ICAM-1 on endothelium, enabling firm adhesion before the cell squeezes out of the vessel. Absent in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.
The squeezing of a leukocyte through the gap between endothelial cells to leave the bloodstream and enter tissue during inflammation. It follows rolling and tight adhesion.
A red-orange fluorescent dye used in staining and microscopy. Auramine-rhodamine stain highlights acid-fast bacteria such as mycobacteria.
Highly reactive oxygen-derived molecules such as superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radical. Phagocytes use them to kill microbes; excess damages DNA, lipids and proteins.
A cytokine that supports the survival and activation of natural killer cells and memory CD8 T cells.
A B-cell signaling enzyme needed for pre-B cell maturation. Mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinemia; inhibited by ibrutinib in B-cell cancers.
Transmission of genes on the X chromosome. In X-linked recessive disease, affected males pass the mutation to all daughters but no sons; there is no male-to-male transmission.
Dry eye from reduced tear production, causing gritty, irritated eyes and corneal damage. Classically seen in Sjogren syndrome.
An autoimmune destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands causing dry eyes and dry mouth. Associated with anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies and lymphoma risk.
A neutrophil granule serine protease that is the target of c-ANCA in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Elevated levels of serum immunoglobulins, polyclonal in chronic infection and autoimmune disease, or monoclonal in plasma cell disorders.
A distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement of the wrist, giving a dinner-fork deformity, typically after falling on an outstretched hand.
Infection with Salmonella, ranging from self-limited gastroenteritis from poultry and eggs to systemic typhoid fever.
A ligament running from the acetabular fossa to the fovea of the femoral head. It carries a small artery that supplies the head in children.
syn: ligament of the head of the femur

def: A benign bony outgrowth from a bone surface. Multiple hereditary exostoses are linked to EXT1 and EXT2 mutations.
A firm subcutaneous nodule over pressure points in rheumatoid arthritis, consisting of central necrosis ringed by palisading histiocytes.
Enlargement of the thymus with lymphoid follicles, seen in myasthenia gravis and some autoimmune disorders.
The double membrane surrounding the nucleus, continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and perforated by nuclear pores. Supported inside by nuclear lamins.
Transmembrane proteins that form tight junctions between epithelial cells, controlling paracellular permeability.
A basement membrane glycoprotein that binds cells to the extracellular matrix through integrins.
Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. Seen in psoriasis, eczema and actinic keratosis.
Loss of connections between keratinocytes, causing intraepidermal blisters. The hallmark of pemphigus vulgaris.
A gram-positive anaerobic rod that lives in hair follicles and contributes to acne vulgaris. Now called Cutibacterium acnes.
A receptor tyrosine kinase that binds insulin-like growth factor 1 and mediates growth hormone's growth-promoting effects.
Organelles in melanocytes where melanin is made and then transferred to keratinocytes.
Melanoma in situ on chronically sun-damaged skin of older adults, appearing as a slowly enlarging irregular brown patch.
A gram-negative bacterium spread by body lice causing trench fever and bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients.
A rapidly growing, friable red capillary proliferation that bleeds easily, seen after trauma and in pregnancy.
A genetically engineered tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin. A thrombolytic for myocardial infarction and stroke.
A potent NSAID given by injection or orally for short-term pain relief. It carries risks of kidney injury, ulcers and bleeding.
Channel proteins in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria and mitochondria that allow passage of small molecules.
Fibrous amniotic strands entangling a fetus, causing limb constriction rings, amputations and craniofacial defects.
Mandibulofacial dysostosis from first pharyngeal arch neural crest defects, causing underdeveloped cheekbones and jaw, downslanting eyes and ear anomalies.
Staphylococcus aureus with thickened cell walls that reduce vancomycin susceptibility. VRSA acquires vanA from enterococci.
A statistical test comparing means across three or more groups by comparing between-group and within-group variance.
A GnRH agonist that after initial stimulation suppresses LH and FSH release.
A GnRH agonist that, given continuously, suppresses gonadotropins. Used for prostate cancer and precocious puberty.
A G-protein-coupled receptor on pituitary gonadotrophs binding gonadotropin-releasing hormone, triggering LH and FSH release.
A nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor that blocks estrogen synthesis. Used for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women; risk of osteoporosis.
A synthetic progestin used for endometrial cancer and to stimulate appetite in cachexia.
The c-Mpl receptor on megakaryocytes and platelets that binds thrombopoietin to drive platelet production. Targeted by romiplostim and eltrombopag.
A monoclonal antibody against the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25), used to prevent transplant rejection.
A cytokine from T cells that supports early hematopoietic progenitors and growth of multiple blood cell lines.
A cytokine from Th1 and NK cells that activates macrophages and promotes MHC expression and Th1 differentiation.
Red cells with irregular spiky projections, seen in abetalipoproteinemia, liver disease and McLeod syndrome.
Inherited red cell membrane defect (spectrin or protein 4.1) giving oval cells and mild hemolysis.
Surgical rerouting of urine after cystectomy, such as an ileal conduit that drains ureters to a stoma on the abdomen.
A histone deacetylase inhibitor used for relapsed multiple myeloma.
A histone deacetylase inhibitor used for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
An enzyme that removes acetyl groups from histones, tightening chromatin and silencing genes.
Membrane transport of two substances in the same direction by one carrier, such as the sodium-glucose cotransporter.
A decoy receptor for RANKL secreted by osteoblasts that blocks osteoclast formation and bone resorption.
Shortness of breath and low oxygen on sitting or standing that improve when lying flat, from right-to-left shunting such as through a patent foramen ovale.
An organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic poisoning.
A first-generation H1 antihistamine used in cold and allergy remedies, causing sedation.
The receptor for IL-4 and IL-13 that drives Th2 differentiation and IgE class switching.
Hydrated magnesium silicate. Used for pleurodesis and associated with granulomas in IV drug users.
Breaks through both DNA strands, repaired by homologous recombination or nonhomologous end joining. Caused by ionizing radiation; defective in ataxia-telangiectasia.
Substances that stimulate cells to divide, such as growth factors and lectins.
Small GTP-binding proteins that relay growth signals from receptor tyrosine kinases to the MAP kinase pathway. Mutations lock them on in many cancers.
The B chain of platelet-derived growth factor, encoded by c-sis. Stimulates fibroblast and smooth muscle growth.
A receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor on mast cells and hematopoietic cells. Activating mutations cause GIST and mastocytosis.
The ligand of c-Kit, supporting survival and growth of hematopoietic progenitors, mast cells and melanocytes.
Factors that activate genes for S-phase entry. Held inactive by hypophosphorylated Rb protein until cyclin-CDK phosphorylation releases them.
Overuse tendinopathy of the wrist extensors at the lateral epicondyle, causing outer elbow pain.
The shallow socket of the scapula that articulates with the humeral head to form the shoulder joint.
The deep fascia enveloping the thigh muscles. Its lateral thickening forms the iliotibial tract.
Ligaments running along the front (anterior) and back (posterior) of the vertebral bodies. The anterior limits hyperextension; the posterior limits hyperflexion.
A uric acid breakdown product in most mammals, used in skin-soothing products.
An oral prodrug converted to 5-fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor. Used for colorectal and breast cancer; causes hand-foot syndrome.
Dilation of the ascending aorta, linked to cystic medial degeneration, Marfan syndrome and tertiary syphilis.
An enzyme activated by calcium-calmodulin that phosphorylates myosin light chains to trigger smooth muscle contraction.
A calcium-binding protein that activates enzymes such as myosin light chain kinase and CaM kinases.
Narrowing of the aorta just above the aortic valve, associated with Williams syndrome and elastin gene deletion.
Brain swelling from severe hypertension causing headache, confusion, seizures and vision loss; reversible with blood pressure control.
Antimicrobials, such as metronidazole and tinidazole, that generate free radicals damaging DNA of anaerobes and protozoa.
A nitroimidazole antimicrobial, similar to metronidazole, used for giardiasis, trichomoniasis, amebiasis and bacterial vaginosis.
A macrolide antibiotic used to treat toxoplasmosis in pregnancy to reduce fetal transmission.
Infection with Cryptococcus neoformans from inhaled pigeon-dropping yeast, causing meningitis in AIDS. India ink shows encapsulated yeast.
A motile, urease-positive gram-negative rod that swarms on agar and causes urinary tract infections.
Fungal organisms in the bloodstream, most often Candida in catheterized or immunosuppressed patients.
A test in which latex beads coated with antibody or antigen clump when the target is present. Used for rheumatoid factor and Cryptococcus antigen.
A sugar component of bacterial peptidoglycan, chitin and glycoproteins.
A bacterial appendage used in conjugation to transfer DNA between cells, encoded by the F plasmid.
Cell surface proteins on antigen-presenting cells that present extracellular peptide to CD4 helper T cells. Encoded by HLA-DP, DQ and DR.
A group D strep now called S. gallolyticus. Causes endocarditis and is associated with colon cancer.
Antiseptics in which iodine is bound to a carrier such as povidone, used to disinfect skin.
Excess fat around the waist and visceral organs, a feature of metabolic syndrome.
The retroviral gene encoding the envelope glycoproteins; in HIV it codes gp120 and gp41.
Cold sores: recurrent HSV-1 vesicles on the lip, reactivated from the trigeminal ganglion.
Large enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. Include variola, vaccinia, molluscum contagiosum and monkeypox.
Gram-negative facultative anaerobic rods that ferment glucose and are oxidase negative. Include E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella, Shigella and Proteus.
A viridans streptococcus that produces dextran from sucrose and causes dental caries.
Hepatic damage from medications or toxins, such as acetaminophen overdose, with patterns of hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed injury.
A second-generation oral cephalosporin used for otitis media and respiratory infections.
A third-generation oral cephalosporin used for uncomplicated gonorrhea and urinary infections.
Chemotherapy, radiation or other treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumor.
Rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the floor of the mouth, usually from a dental infection, which can obstruct the airway.
Recovery of immune function after cause of suppression is treated, such as after antiretroviral therapy in HIV.
Paradoxical worsening of an infection as the recovering immune system reacts to pathogens after starting antiretroviral therapy in HIV.
A mosquito-borne alphavirus infection causing fever and severe, often prolonged, joint pain.
A combination of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors used for HIV treatment and as pre-exposure prophylaxis.
Low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone density in female athletes.
A carbapenem antibiotic with broad gram-negative and anaerobic coverage.
HSV infection of the cornea producing a branching dendritic ulcer, treated with topical antivirals.
Bilateral granulomatous uveitis after penetrating trauma to one eye, as exposed uveal antigens trigger autoimmunity.
The ability to recognize and repeat spoken words, tested in audiometry.
Antibiotics such as clindamycin that bind the 50S ribosome. Cover anaerobes; risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis.
Two or more consecutive spontaneous miscarriages, with causes including antiphospholipid syndrome and chromosomal abnormalities.
An aminoglycoside antibiotic active against resistant gram-negative bacteria and mycobacteria. Toxic to ears and kidneys.
An antibody-based test using an enzyme-linked label to detect antigen or antibody by color change, as in ELISA.
Meningitis from Listeria monocytogenes in neonates, older adults and immunocompromised patients; treated with ampicillin.
Infection with Klebsiella pneumoniae causing pneumonia, urinary infection and liver abscess, notably in alcoholics and diabetics.
Shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Nasociliary involvement (Hutchinson sign) predicts eye disease.
Attachment of a virus to host receptors and penetration into the cell, as in HIV binding CD4 and CCR5.
A less pathogenic relative of HIV found mainly in West Africa, naturally resistant to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
An RNA virus spread by the fecal-oral route that causes acute hepatitis. Carries high mortality in pregnancy.
A mosquito-borne flavivirus causing breakbone fever with fever, retro-orbital pain and thrombocytopenia.
An HIV protease inhibitor that blocks cleavage of viral polyproteins.
A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV that binds reverse transcriptase directly. Risk of rash and hepatotoxicity.
Heterocyclic compounds forming the core of folic acid and tetrahydrobiopterin.
A fluoroquinolone antibiotic inhibiting DNA gyrase.
A respiratory fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
Automatic repetition of words just heard, seen in autism, schizophrenia and Tourette syndrome.
Rigid posture held for a long time, with waxy flexibility, seen in catatonia.
A wakefulness-promoting drug for narcolepsy that acts by inhibiting dopamine reuptake.
An adenosine deaminase inhibitor used for hairy cell leukemia.
Alkylating agents, like mechlorethamine and cyclophosphamide, that crosslink DNA.
A common antiseptic and solvent. Ingestion causes ketosis without acidosis and CNS depression.
A platinum chemotherapy that forms DNA crosslinks, used in colorectal cancer. Causes cold-triggered neuropathy.
Chemotherapy drugs such as irinotecan and topotecan that trap topoisomerase I on DNA, causing strand breaks.
A receptor tyrosine kinase on endothelial cells that drives angiogenesis. Blocked by drugs such as sorafenib.
Fungal lung infection caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii in AIDS, with diffuse ground-glass opacities.
An enzyme in cholesterol and ergosterol synthesis, inhibited by terbinafine.
The insect vector of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness).
An arsenic-containing drug for late-stage African sleeping sickness with CNS involvement.
An ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor used for African sleeping sickness and for facial hirsutism.
An antiparasitic used for early-stage African trypanosomiasis.
A protozoan causing mucocutaneous leishmaniasis in South America.
The insect vector of Leishmania.
A heavy metal in pentavalent form for leishmaniasis.
A pentavalent antimony drug used for leishmaniasis.
An antimalarial that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, combined with atovaquone.
Flatworms, including flukes and tapeworms.
A toxic gas that inhibits cytochrome oxidase, like cyanide.
E. coli strains with P fimbriae causing most urinary tract infections.
A marine gram-negative bacterium causing watery diarrhea after raw seafood.
MRI imaging of the bile and pancreatic ducts without contrast injection.
Persistent abdominal pain or dyspepsia after gallbladder removal.
A semisynthetic opioid agonist for moderate to severe pain.
A sugar acid in bacterial peptidoglycan.
A gram-negative rod now called Klebsiella aerogenes, causing hospital-acquired infections.
An anthelmintic that blocks microtubule polymerization in worms, used for pinworm and roundworm.
The apoE variant with poor receptor binding, linked to familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.
An IL-1 receptor antagonist used for rheumatoid arthritis and autoinflammatory diseases.
A ligament binding the front of the distal tibia and fibula in the ankle syndesmosis; injured in high ankle sprains.
A test in which lymphocytes from two people are cultured together; proliferation shows HLA mismatch.
Histologic stains that deposit silver on organisms or fibers, such as for Legionella, Pneumocystis and reticulin.
The oral live attenuated poliovirus vaccine, giving gut mucosal immunity but with rare vaccine-derived paralysis.
Impulse control disorder of deliberate fire-setting for tension relief.
Gastroenteritis from norovirus, a calicivirus, causing vomiting and diarrhea outbreaks.
Cell surface proteins mediating adhesion, including integrins, selectins, cadherins and immunoglobulin superfamily members.
